sketches.title: Parent-Teacher Nightmare
sketches.premise: The school has written a bland report about an adult. Turn it into the kind of comment that makes a parent sit down slowly. Keep the report’s tiny truth alive while sending its meaning somewhere gloriously unhelpful.
sketches.criterion: The move must keep the report’s exact everyday observation true, without claiming the opposite or quietly deleting it.
sketches.move_shape: Write one school-report comment under 90 characters, adding a shocking interpretation, warning, or consequence; example: “He shares equipment well, especially evidence.”
sketches.first_card: She remembers to bring a pen.

sketches.title: Progress Report from Hell
sketches.premise: Each card is a painfully ordinary note about an adult. Write the next line of the report: a prediction that makes the small fact feel like the opening scene of a disaster, while the fact still stands. The teacher is calm; the implications are not.
sketches.criterion: The move must preserve the card’s observation as true while making a believable future consequence from it.
sketches.move_shape: Write one forecast under 90 characters, beginning with “Next term…”; example: “Next term, he may stop naming the voices.”

sketches.title: Remarkable Effort
sketches.premise: You are marking adult pupils whose ordinary habits deserve suspiciously generous praise. Recast the card as a glowing report comment, keeping the stated fact true but making the compliment wildly specific. Gold stars are cheap; insinuation is free.
sketches.criterion: The move must still support the card’s fact while praising it through an invented achievement, talent, or hidden motive.
sketches.move_shape: Write one glowing report comment under 90 characters; example: “She arrives early, giving the building time to prepare.”

sketches.title: Behaviour Watch
sketches.premise: A school report records one harmless fact about an adult. Turn it into a formal behaviour note that sounds polite, measured, and deeply alarming. Keep the fact intact; the fun is making a tiny habit look like a case file.
sketches.criterion: The move must leave the card’s fact true and frame it as evidence of a risk, pattern, or incident.
sketches.move_shape: Write one official-sounding warning under 90 characters; example: “He labels his lunch; staff are monitoring the system.”

sketches.title: Reference Request
sketches.premise: Someone has asked the school for a reference about an adult, and you have only one dull report fact. Write the reference line that technically answers the question while making the reader wonder what was left out. The truth gets a seat; your tact gets pushed out the window.
sketches.criterion: The move must retain the card’s fact and present it as a relevant judgment about the person.
sketches.move_shape: Write one reference sentence under 90 characters; example: “He is reliable when the cupboard is already locked.”

sketches.title: School Newsletter
sketches.premise: Turn a flat school-report fact about an adult into a cheerful newsletter item. It must sound suitable for families while the same truth quietly suggests a scandal, secret, or heroic cover-up. Keep it mild: raised eyebrows, not police tape.
sketches.criterion: The move must keep the card’s fact true while placing it inside an invented school-news story.
sketches.move_shape: Write one upbeat newsletter item under 90 characters; example: “Our tidy treasurer has made the missing money feel welcome.”
